A campus full of possibilities.

Read a mind. Train a memory. Make a rhythm. Think with an object.

MIND(s) can bring a poem, a molecular model, a chant, a sporting action and a philosophical argument into the same common course. These 28 candidates give colleagues concrete ways to contribute.

Memorize20 min estimate

Learn a poem by heart

Emily Dickinson · The Brain—is wider than the Sky

Make memory part of the encounter with a work about mind.

Literature & languages / Music & performance / Learning & access

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. An authorized poem text; paper.

  1. Read the poem aloud or silently.
  2. Learn a short passage using rhythm, imagery or repetition.
  3. Reconstruct it from memory, then mark changes against the text.

Students produce: A marked comparison of the remembered and printed passage.

Use private recall or paired recitation; public performance is optional. This is not a memory ranking.

The Brain—is wider than the Sky

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Test & model20 min estimate

Compare two ways of studying

Roediger & Karpicke · Test-Enhanced Learning (2006)

Turn memorization into a testable teaching problem.

Learning & access / Psychology & neuroscience / Mathematics & computing

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Two short instructor-written passages; a timer; next-class recall sheet.

  1. Alternate rereading and closed-text retrieval across two passages.
  2. Switch the passage assignments across small groups.
  3. Compare delayed recall next class using a common scoring guide.

Students produce: An aggregate comparison and a short account of confounds.

The published study supports retrieval practice; this short adaptation is not a replication or a diagnostic test. Do not collect named performance records for research.

Roediger & Karpicke · study abstract

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Listen & watch25 min estimate

Hear how a text is preserved

UNESCO · Tradition of Vedic chanting

Connect sacred text, sound, exactness and trained memory.

Religion & philosophy / Literature & languages / Music & performance

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. UNESCO documentation; a recording with identified performers and context.

  1. Introduce the named tradition and recording.
  2. Annotate repeated sounds, pitch patterns and correction procedures visible in the documentation.
  3. Compare oral transmission with a printed passage.

Students produce: An annotated listening timeline and transmission comparison.

Study the documented practice; any participatory recitation should be developed with a qualified practitioner. The proposal does not claim a generic memory benefit from all chant.

UNESCO · Tradition of Vedic chanting

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Perform & move15 min estimate

Make a room sound together

Vickhoff et al. · Music structure and singers’ heart-rate variability (2013)

Pair the experience of coordinated singing with evidence about bodily timing.

Music & performance / Psychology & neuroscience / Mathematics & computing

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. A facilitator’s short neutral vocal pattern; the study’s published figures.

  1. Speak or hum a short neutral pattern at comfortable volume.
  2. Repeat with a shared conductor cue; offer a listening role.
  3. Inspect the study’s published breathing and heart-rate figures.

Students produce: A description separating heard coordination from measured physiology.

Use ordinary breathing. Classroom synchrony does not demonstrate shared consciousness, and no participant biosensors are required.

Vickhoff et al. · original study

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Perform & move20 min estimate

Keep one pattern; shift another

Steve Reich · Clapping Music (1972)

Let musical structure become a problem of attention, timing and relation.

Music & performance / Mathematics & computing / Movement & sport

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Authorized score or recording; an instructor-made beginner pattern.

  1. Hear a passage of Reich’s work.
  2. Keep one simple pattern fixed while a second group shifts its starting point.
  3. Draw the repeating cycle and mark the return to alignment.

Students produce: A cycle diagram linked to the performed pattern.

The beginner exercise is an adaptation, not a reproduction of the score. Tapping or visual cue tracking can replace clapping.

Steve Reich · composer’s notes

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Listen & watch40 min estimate

Collective trance: music, movement and context

Healing Dance Music of the Kalahari San · Smithsonian Folkways

Treat trance as a serious subject of cultural and musical inquiry.

Anthropology & society / Religion & philosophy / Music & performance

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Licensed recording or available preview; album notes.

  1. Identify the people, occasion and documentation behind the recording.
  2. Trace the musical features described in the notes alongside the recording.
  3. Separate participant meanings, the recorder’s interpretation and physiological hypotheses.

Students produce: A three-column evidence account tied to specific moments.

The recording documents a particular healing tradition. A listening session does not recreate it. A practitioner-led campus event would require an invitation, collaboration and agreed terms.

Smithsonian Folkways · recording and album notes

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Test & model30 min estimate

Read a collective event as data

Konvalinka et al. · Synchronized arousal in a fire-walking ritual (2011)

Bring ethnography and quantitative analysis into the same class.

Anthropology & society / Psychology & neuroscience / Mathematics & computing

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Published graphs and methods; no live ritual reenactment.

  1. Locate the performers and spectator groups in the study design.
  2. Mark the shared time patterns in published heart-rate plots.
  3. Distinguish correlation, social relationship and the authors’ interpretation.

Students produce: An annotated figure with a bounded claim.

Use the published case, not classroom fire-walking. Physiological synchrony does not by itself establish collective trance or one group mind.

Konvalinka et al. · original research

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Test & model15 min estimate

Catch reading competing with color

J. R. Stroop · Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions (1935)

Make automaticity and attention immediately observable.

Psychology & neuroscience / Literature & languages / Learning & access

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Instructor-made congruent and incongruent color-word sheets.

  1. Name colors on a short practice sheet.
  2. Compare congruent and incongruent sheets with order varied across volunteers.
  3. Record aggregate time and errors, then identify practice and language effects.

Students produce: A simple results table and a limitations note.

Offer the published dataset or a non-color analysis role. The exercise is not an intelligence test; color perception and reading fluency affect participation.

Stroop · original article

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Test & model15 min estimate

Make a mark disappear

Exploratorium · Blind Spot

Connect the physical eye with a constructed visual experience.

Natural sciences / Psychology & neuroscience / Art & making

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. A dot-and-cross card; ruler; source demonstration.

  1. Follow the museum’s dot-and-cross demonstration.
  2. Mark the viewing distance at which the dot disappears.
  3. Compare the observation with the source’s retinal explanation.

Students produce: A labeled diagram of the setup and a description of the effect.

Offer diagram analysis as an alternative. This demonstration is not a vision screening.

Exploratorium · science demonstration

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Make & curate25 min estimate

Think with a strip of paper

Lygia Clark · Caminhando (Walking)

An object can make choice and embodied action visible.

Art & making / Mathematics & computing / Religion & philosophy

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Paper strips, tape and scissors; artwork documentation.

  1. Study Clark’s documented work.
  2. Make and cut a paper Möbius strip as a clearly labeled classroom response.
  3. Record how each action changes the available next action.

Students produce: The altered paper form with an action sequence.

Use pre-cut forms or a partner cutting role where useful. The response is not the original artwork or evidence for a specific consciousness theory.

Caminhando (Walking)

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Make & curate35 min estimate

Mind as a printed object

Jikji · surviving 1377 metal-type edition

Connect Buddhist teaching, typography, material history and transmission.

Archives & history / Religion & philosophy / Art & making / Literature & languages

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Digital facsimile or authorized reproduction; English translation.

  1. Inspect a reproduced page and the fuller title.
  2. Read a short translated passage beside the page.
  3. Write a museum label distinguishing the teaching from the printing history.

Students produce: A 100-word object label with source and translation credits.

Use reproductions; do not imply a campus holding of the original. Jikji is the oldest surviving movable-metal-type book, not the first printing of any kind.

Jikji: the book and its printing history

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Read & compare30 min estimate

Translate heart, mind and self

MIND(s) · multilingual word collection and dictionaries

Make translation a campus-wide contribution rather than a decorative word list.

Literature & languages / Religion & philosophy / Learning & access

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Three dictionary records; human recordings; source-language readers if available.

  1. Choose three documented terms.
  2. List the senses supported by each dictionary.
  3. Translate a short instructor-selected sentence and annotate what each choice loses.

Students produce: A small bilingual or multilingual translation display.

Do not treat a dictionary gloss as an entire culture’s philosophy. Contributions from fluent readers need credit.

마음 maeum: Korean lexical record

Listen & watch25 min estimate

Mind in a signed language

HandSpeak · ASL MIND; ASL University · THINK

Bring language, movement and access into the theme.

Literature & languages / Learning & access / Music & performance

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Provider-hosted demonstrations; captions and written definitions.

  1. View a documented sign and its explanation.
  2. Describe handshape, location and movement using the source.
  3. Compare the meaning with an English dictionary entry.

Students produce: An annotated account of one sign, with its provider credited.

For instruction and participant practice, involve a qualified ASL educator. ASL is not universal sign language; a sign’s location is not a signer’s theory of mind.

MIND in American Sign Language

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Perform & move30 min estimate

Put the mind–body dispute on stage

Elisabeth of Bohemia and Descartes · correspondence (1643)

Let theatre clarify an argument and its stakes.

Religion & philosophy / Music & performance / Literature & languages

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Authorized translated excerpts; role cards based on the text.

  1. Assign readers the two correspondents and a textual narrator.
  2. Read an exchange without rewriting its claims.
  3. Restage it with pauses marking premises, objections and replies.

Students produce: An annotated performance script.

The staging is interpretive. Keep the historical participants’ claims separate from newly written commentary.

Stanford Encyclopedia · Elisabeth of Bohemia

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Make & curate40 min estimate

Make two versions of one awakening

Zhuangzi · butterfly dream

Use film form to examine how certainty is produced.

Art & making / Literature & languages / Religion & philosophy

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Chapter 2 in translation; storyboard paper or a phone camera.

  1. Read the dream episode closely.
  2. Storyboard the same moment from two viewpoints.
  3. Label the framing or editing choice that changes the apparent identity.

Students produce: Two six-frame storyboards or brief silent sequences.

Identify the translation and label the film as an adaptation. A simulation interpretation is not the text’s established conclusion.

Zhuangzi, chapter 2: the butterfly dream

Perform & move25 min estimate

Watch skilled action become intelligible

Zhuangzi · Cook Ding; a simple coached movement

Connect athletic and musical expertise with philosophical accounts of skill.

Movement & sport / Music & performance / Religion & philosophy

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Chapter 3; a low-impact movement or instrumental phrase chosen by a facilitator.

  1. Read the description of Cook Ding’s practice.
  2. Observe an experienced performer demonstrate one simple movement.
  3. Compare the performer’s explanation with a novice’s sequence description.

Students produce: A close comparison of text and demonstration.

Use seated or observational participation. The example is an analogy, not proof that one philosophy explains all expertise.

Zhuangzi, chapter 3: Nourishing the Lord of Life

Listen & watch30 min estimate

Annotate attention in a sporting action

Visual attention in basketball shooting · research review

Give athletics a substantive role in thinking about perception and training.

Movement & sport / Psychology & neuroscience / Mathematics & computing

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. An authorized or consented demonstration video; published study diagrams.

  1. Mark phases of a shot in a short recording.
  2. Compare the annotations with the review’s account of visual attention.
  3. Distinguish a visible head direction from a measured eye movement.

Students produce: A video annotation and measurement plan.

Video alone is not eye tracking. This is not a prescription to change an athlete’s technique.

Research of visual attention in basketball shooting: A systematic review with meta-analysis

Test & model25 min estimate

Hold the numbers steady; change the words

Tversky & Kahneman · The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice (1981)

Connect judgment with public communication and quantitative reasoning.

Economics & public life / Mathematics & computing / Psychology & neuroscience

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Two instructor-written equivalent budget scenarios; private response slips.

  1. Verify that both scenarios have identical numerical outcomes.
  2. Present one framing to each group and record anonymous choices.
  3. Reveal the alternate wording and compare the results with the paper.

Students produce: A numerical equivalence check and aggregate choice table.

A small classroom result may differ from published findings. Avoid treating political disagreement as a cognitive defect.

Tversky & Kahneman · original paper

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Read & compare40 min estimate

Read the self through a social world

W. E. B. Du Bois · The Souls of Black Folk

Connect mind with history, power, identity and musical form.

Anthropology & society / Economics & public life / Literature & languages / Music & performance

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Opening chapter and an authorized musical example from The Sorrow Songs.

  1. Trace the opening chapter’s account of double consciousness.
  2. Locate a musical or formal feature in the work.
  3. Write a passage-based comparison of individual experience and social judgment.

Students produce: A short textual analysis with precise references.

Do not require personal disclosure or ask students to represent a racial group. Preserve the historical specificity of the concept.

The Souls of Black Folk

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Make & curate30 min estimate

Build the scale between molecule and action

RCSB PDB-101 · Acetylcholine Receptor

Give chemistry and biochemistry a concrete object in the study of mind.

Natural sciences / Psychology & neuroscience / Art & making

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. The receptor’s structure viewer or printed diagram; modeling materials.

  1. Locate the binding site and membrane channel in the model.
  2. Arrange a sequence from transmitter binding to channel opening.
  3. Mark the explanatory gap between this mechanism and a complete account of experience.

Students produce: A molecular-to-cellular diagram with explicit scale labels.

A molecular model explains a mechanism, not consciousness as a whole. Use a physical or printed model when the viewer is inaccessible.

RCSB PDB-101 · Acetylcholine Receptor

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Test & model35 min estimate

Read coordination without a brain

Levin and collaborators · information structures in aneural tissues

Connect living organization with the language of cognition.

Natural sciences / Mathematics & computing / Religion & philosophy

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Published figures; a small instructor-made network dataset.

  1. Identify what the study actually measures.
  2. Draw a network from the sample dataset.
  3. Separate measured coordination from a claim about felt experience.

Students produce: An annotated network and two differently scoped claims.

The sample is an instructional model, not tissue data. No live biological experiment is proposed here.

Revealing non-trivial information structures in aneural biological tissues via functional connectivity

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Read & compare35 min estimate

Compare performance with a claim to experience

Alan Turing · Computing Machinery and Intelligence

Make computing part of the common course without equating fluency with consciousness.

Mathematics & computing / Religion & philosophy / Economics & public life

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Turing’s article; instructor-written illustrative transcripts.

  1. Read Turing’s test proposal.
  2. Compare two clearly labeled illustrative transcripts against stated criteria.
  3. Write separate conclusions about performance and subjective experience.

Students produce: A test specification with a limits statement.

Synthetic transcripts must be labeled. No private student writing needs to be sent to an AI system.

Turing · 1950 article

Test & model20 min estimate

Take the notebook seriously

Clark & Chalmers · The Extended Mind

Bring everyday tools and accessibility into the philosophical account.

Mathematics & computing / Learning & access / Religion & philosophy

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Short paper excerpt; a notebook or task checklist.

  1. Read the paper’s notebook example.
  2. Complete a short planning task with an external checklist.
  3. Diagram the roles played by person, tool and environment.

Students produce: A system diagram and a passage-based argument.

This is an illustration of a disputed thesis, not a test proving that tools are conscious.

Clark & Chalmers · The Extended Mind

Perform & move25 min estimate

Make a record of directed attention

William James · attention; a campus soundwalk

Let place, sound and attention enter the same observation.

Environment & place / Music & performance / Psychology & neuroscience

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. A brief James excerpt; a chosen accessible location; notebook.

  1. Listen briefly without a recording device.
  2. Repeat while attending to one sound category.
  3. Compare the two written inventories.

Students produce: Two sound inventories with a note on the change of method.

Offer a stationary indoor location and a visual observation alternative. The exercise illustrates attention; it does not prove a restorative effect of nature.

Make & curate30 min estimate

Infer a mind from an object

Smithsonian · early tools, images and instruments

Connect archaeology, material evidence and the limits of interpretation.

Environment & place / Archives & history / Natural sciences / Art & making

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Museum object records and images; material or replica examples if available.

  1. Choose one documented early object.
  2. Describe its observable features before interpreting them.
  3. Write separate labels for a supported capacity and an uncertain belief.

Students produce: A two-part museum label distinguishing evidence and inference.

Do not present an object as a transcript of its maker’s beliefs or living peoples as replicas of prehistoric societies.

Compare observation and interpretation on a journey

Hyecho’s pilgrimage account · translation credited to Matty Wegehaupt and collaborators

Connect travel, religious practice and the limits of knowing other people.

Archives & history / Literature & languages / Religion & philosophy / Environment & place

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Authorized translated passage and the Michigan project’s context.

  1. Read a short passage with its translation credit.
  2. Mark direct observation separately from reported information and interpretation.

Make & curate45 min estimate

Curate a campus history of attention

Lawrence’s Lux · public concert programs and archival collections

Make the campus’s own intellectual and performance history part of MIND(s).

Archives & history / Music & performance / Anthropology & society

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. Three public items selected from Lux with a librarian or archivist.

  1. Choose three public objects around one practice, such as recital preparation or collective listening.
  2. Record creator, date, audience and context for each.
  3. Write an exhibition introduction linking the objects through an explicit argument.

Students produce: A three-object exhibition proposal.

The linked catalog identifies collections, not a preselected set of objects. Selection and reuse terms still need checking; no private records are included.

Read & compare15 min estimate

Observe attention during a short reading

Dhammapada · verses on mind

Pair a text on mental cultivation with a modest observation of attention.

Religion & philosophy / Learning & access / Literature & languages

Source
Activity, materials & teaching notes

Materials. A credited translation of verses 33–43; a neutral short prose passage.

  1. Read the selected verses in their Buddhist context.
  2. Read the prose silently for two minutes, noting a return of attention if it occurs.
  3. Distinguish the textual teaching from this classroom observation.

Students produce: A private observation note and a textual annotation.

Participation can be textual only. This is not a therapeutic intervention or a complete Buddhist meditation practice.

Dhammapada 33–43: Cittavagga

Proposed teaching adaptation · not classroom-tested here.

Many kinds of expertise belong here.

These are invitations to contribute, not claims of departmental participation. Connections draw on Lawrence’s public collections directory and academic and campus resources.

Conservatory, theatre, dance & athletics

Bring ensemble timing, vocal practice, gesture, interpretation and trained movement. Performance can be both a work to study and a way of investigating mind.

Performance candidates

Sciences, mathematics & computing

Bring molecules, perception, measurement, networks and models. Clarify the difference between an observation, a mechanism and an explanation.

Science candidates

Humanities, languages & social inquiry

Bring translations, religious practices, poetry, argument, history, judgment and accounts of the social self.

Social and cultural candidates

Libraries, galleries, learning & campus life

Bring public collections, accessible formats, study practices, exhibitions and spaces for shared attention. A small display or event can make the proposal tangible.

Learning and access candidates

From a candidate to a shared experience

Choose a work, pair two kinds of expertise, and prepare one short encounter. A faculty demonstration could combine a brief reading, an activity and an example of student work. The shortlist is a starting point for that conversation.

Sources document works or research; the activities here are editorial proposals, not validated lesson plans. Provider recordings and scores remain with their rights holders. Some candidates need a specialist facilitator, practitioner collaboration or a licensed excerpt.
